(CNN) -- Academy Award-winning composer Maurice Jarre, who scored movies including "Doctor Zhivago" and "Lawrence of Arabia" among others, died Sunday from cancer in Los Angeles. He was 84. Movie composer Maurice Jarre pictured at the Berlin International Film Festival last month. Jarre enjoyed an illustrious career, working with Hollywood directing legends including John Huston, Alfred Hitchcock and, most notably, David Lean. Fellow French composer Alexandre Desplat, who interviewed Jarre for The Screening Room at the Berlin International Film Festival last month, told CNN Monday: "Maurice was an immense artist, an incredible symphonist, a magician of the melody and a benevolent human being."  Watch tribute to Maurice Jarre » . Jarre won Oscars in 1963 and 1966 for his collaborations on the Lean movies "Lawrence of Arabia" and "Doctor Zhivago" respectively. He then mustered a further six Oscar nominations but his third award came once again through a further collaboration with Lean on " A Passage to India" in 1984. He then swapped orchestral composition to become a pioneer of electronic scoring, working on the music for, among others, "Ghost," "Witness," "Dead Poet's Society" and "Fatal Attraction." At the same time his son Jean-Michel Jarre became one of the world's best known electronic musicians with global hits such as "Oxygene" and huge outdoor concerts. His final movie composition was for the 2000 film "I Dreamed of Africa." Jarre's career included symphonies, ballet and theatre but it was for his 150 film scores that he was presented with an honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival last month - almost half a century after producer Sam Spiegel hired him to work on "Lawrence of Arabia." Festival director Dieter Kosslick said in a statement late last year: "Film composers often are in the shadows of great directors and acting stars. It's different with Maurice Jarre; the music of 'Doctor Zhivago,' like much of his work, is world-famous and remains unforgotten in the history of cinema." Speaking in Berlin to double-Oscar nominee Desplat -- who himself scored "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" and "The Queen" -- Jarre said: "I never really had a 'bust-up' with a good director. A good director will always find an intellectual understanding. And that's what was great - I had an opportunity with all these people. I don't think I can say that I ever worked with a bad director." But Jarre also said that directing legends of the rank of Huston and Hitchock had disappeared and no longer existed, adding: "The only problem is now, there is more and more bad music that goes 'dang dang dang dang dang...' So...it's better to turn off the music, and listen to a concert of Mozart." Senior producer Neil Curry and associate producer Lidz-Ama Appiah contributed to this report.

Jarre, shown last month at the Berlin International Film Festival, had a distinguished career in cinema, collaborating with some of Hollywood’s most celebrated directors, among them John Huston, Alfred Hitchcock and, above all, David Lean.

French composer Alexandre Desplat, who interviewed Jarre for “The Screening Room” during the Berlin festival, told CNN on Monday: “Maurice was an immense artist, an incredible symphonist, a magician of the melody and a benevolent human being.”

Jarre received Academy Awards in 1963 and 1966 for his work with Lean on “Lawrence of Arabia” and “Doctor Zhivago,” respectively. He went on to earn six more Oscar nominations before winning a third time, again for a Lean film, “A Passage to India,” in 1984.

Later in his career, Jarre moved away from traditional orchestral writing and became an early innovator in electronic film scoring. His music was featured in films such as “Ghost,” “Witness,” “Dead Poets Society” and “Fatal Attraction.” During the same period, his son, Jean-Michel Jarre, rose to international fame as one of the best-known electronic musicians, with worldwide successes including “Oxygene” and large-scale outdoor concerts.

Jarre’s last film score was for the 2000 movie “I Dreamed of Africa.”

Although his body of work also included symphonies, ballet and theater, Jarre was honored mainly for his 150 film scores when he received an honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival last month. The tribute came nearly 50 years after producer Sam Spiegel brought him on to compose the music for “Lawrence of Arabia.”

Festival director Dieter Kosslick said in a statement late the previous year that film composers are often overshadowed by major directors and stars, but that Jarre was an exception. He noted that the music from “Doctor Zhivago,” like much of Jarre’s output, had become famous around the world and remained an enduring part of film history.

In Berlin, speaking with Desplat — himself a two-time Oscar nominee whose credits include “The Curious Case of Benjamin Button” and “The Queen” — Jarre said he had never truly had a serious falling-out with a talented director. He said a good director would always be able to reach an intellectual understanding, and that he felt fortunate to have worked with all the directors he did. He added that he did not believe he had ever collaborated with a bad director.

Jarre also remarked that legendary filmmakers on the level of Huston and Hitchcock were no longer around. He added that, in his view, much current film music had become increasingly poor, describing it as repetitive “dang dang dang dang dang,” and suggested it might be better to turn the music off and listen to a Mozart concert instead.

Senior producer Neil Curry and associate producer Lidz-Ama Appiah contributed to the report.

“Today, many directors are afraid of silence,” Jarre said in one interview, reflecting on changes in the industry. He also spoke of the growing pressure on composers to imitate existing “temp” scores rather than create original musical identities for films, lamenting that the practice could make movie music sound interchangeable.

Even so, Jarre remained active well into later life. His **final feature-film score** was for **“I Dreamed of Africa”** in 2000, starring Kim Basinger. Though he composed less frequently in his final years, his reputation only deepened, particularly among filmmakers and younger composers who regarded him as one of the masters of the craft.

In February 2009, only weeks before his death, Jarre was honored at the **Berlin International Film Festival**, where he received the **Honorary Golden Bear** for lifetime achievement. The festival tribute celebrated not only his famous themes but also the breadth of his work and his influence on the language of cinema. Frail but warmly received, Jarre appeared moved by the recognition.

Jarre’s personal life was also connected to the world of music. He was the father of **Jean-Michel Jarre**, the pioneering electronic musician, as well as screenwriter Kevin Jarre and daughter Stéfanie Jarre. His own later-career embrace of electronics, though distinct from his son’s work, reflected a similar curiosity about sound and technology.

Maurice Jarre leaves behind an extraordinary musical legacy: melodies that became inseparable from the images they accompanied, and scores that helped audiences feel the immensity of deserts, revolutions, romances and moral choices. His music did not merely decorate films; it gave them emotional architecture.

For generations of moviegoers, the first notes of “Lawrence of Arabia” or “Lara’s Theme” remain enough to summon an entire world.
